A statement writes each account once, followed by the nonces of its shares in rising order, about 8 bytes a share; there is exactly one way to write a set of shares, and any other is refused. A proposal carries each share once, however many statements hold it, in one table where each share is marked with the statements that hold it; read back, every statement is exactly as its validator signed it. So a proposal grows with the number of shares, not with shares times validators. Each validator counts at most 10 times the shares wanted per epoch, and never more than 250,000, and refuses the rest until the next checkpoint. At the checkpoint, a convicted staked validator loses everything its account holds in stake (staked, unstaking and waiting to be released), moved to the forfeited account; a convicted seat loses its seat. Shor’s algorithm breaks the elliptic-cur: Shor’s algorithm breaks the elliptic-curve signatures most cryptocurrencies use, but not hash functions. Against a hash function, a quantum computer can at best search faster with Grover’s algorithm, which halves the effective number of bits. Orien’s one-time signatures use the parameters of the one-time layer of SLH-DSA-192, NIST’s security category 3, with BLAKE3 in place of SHA-2 or SHAKE: 192-bit chain values, leaving about 96 bits against a quantum search. One-time keys add a second layer: an account’s next key is revealed only when it signs, and is used for exactly one order, so there is never a long-lived public key for an attacker to work on.

Validators agree on the checkpoint with: Validators agree on the checkpoint with Tendermint [2], rule for rule. In each round a proposer, drawn by weight from a seed taken from the previous checkpoint, proposes a checkpoint together with the statements it merges. Validators check it by recomputing it from the statements, prevote, then precommit; a checkpoint precommitted by more than two thirds of the weight is decided, and the next epoch begins. The rule of locking on a precommitted value keeps two different checkpoints from ever being decided for one epoch, as long as no more than a third of the weight is faulty.
